answer.summary: Andy Raskin defines strategic narrative as a CEO’s unifying story for the company—guiding marketing, sales, product, and other decisions. Unlike category creation focused on naming a product category, strategic narrative focuses on the story and movement; the category may be part of that story, but is not the same thing.

sections.heading: What strategic narrative means
sections.content: Raskin describes it as one story the CEO uses to drive success in marketing, sales, and product, and as a strategic north star for the roadmap, fundraising, recruiting, and more. He says it has a particular structure, contrasting it with the “arrogant doctor” pitch: identify a pain, present a solution as treatment, and explain why it is better than alternatives.

sections.heading: How it differs from creating a product category
sections.content: Raskin says category creation is often reduced to choosing a few words that supposedly make a company seem different. He argues that the name alone is not what makes the idea compelling: Gong’s “revenue intelligence” became meaningful because of the story behind it, and its CEO later suggested the name itself could have been different. Strategic narrative instead emphasizes the broader story or movement. A category can express or accompany that movement, but Raskin sees the two as nearly orthogonal; if the movement becomes recognized as a category, that is a bonus. HubSpot’s inbound movement, for example, remained a constant even as the company’s category labels changed.

sections.content: Raskin calls it one story the CEO uses to drive marketing, sales, and product, and as a north star for the roadmap, fundraising, recruiting, and more. Its structure starts with a shift from an old game to a new game, defining new rules and a movement customers can join—not simply presenting a problem and pitching the company’s solution as a better treatment. Salesforce’s “software is over” and “new world called the cloud” is his archetypal example.

sections.heading: How it differs from creating a product category

He says a label alone will not make a company seem different; the category can be shorthand for the larger narrative, or a bonus if the movement becomes a category. He describes narrative and category as potentially orthogonal: HubSpot’s inbound movement persisted while the company’s category identification changed from marketing automation toward CRM. For Gong, he says the story behind revenue intelligence mattered more than the exact name.

answer.summary: Andy Raskin defines strategic narrative as a CEO’s unifying story and strategic north star. It focuses on the shift in the world and the movement it creates; a product category name may help express that story, but the name alone is not the narrative.

sections.heading: What strategic narrative means
sections.content: Raskin describes it as one story the CEO uses to drive success across marketing and sales and to guide product, fundraising, recruiting, and more. It has a particular structure: rather than the “arrogant doctor” pitch—present a problem, offer a solution, and explain why it is better—it starts with a shift from an old game to a new game and defines a movement. His example is Salesforce framing the move from owned-and-maintained software to the cloud as a new world with new rules.

sections.heading: How it differs from creating a product category
sections.content: Raskin’s distinction is that category creation is often reduced to finding a few words for a category, as if the label alone will make a company seem different. He argues that the story behind the label matters more: Gong’s “revenue intelligence” became meaningful through its story, and its CEO later said the name could have been different. Strategic narrative focuses on the broader story or movement; a category name can serve as shorthand for it, or emerge as a bonus, but is not the central goal. Raskin says the movement can also persist across categories: HubSpot’s inbound narrative remained a constant as its category identification changed.
